name: Yara Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a blasthole drill operator at Kalder, a big open-pit iron ore mine. I drill the holes the blasting crew loads with explosives, about thirty holes a shift, each one fifteen metres deep. Last year they made two of our drills semi-autonomous, so now I sit in one and keep an eye on the other on a tablet. I love that part, honestly, and I hate the drive in, an hour on a gravel road before sunrise.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a shared house in Rookwood, with two nurses from the clinic. I'm still paying off the loan for my mining course, and I send my little brother money for his football fees, so I've got maybe a week or two of savings. I use AI every day, for everything, my budget, my study, even planning the drill pattern sometimes. In my spare time I'm learning to code, badly, off videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, I'd be a little disappointed. I was looking forward to the interesting version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, because a lot of the AI talk is sales talk. At work I'd tell people the tools are still handy, like I'd show them how I plan my week with it. Online I might post a meme about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep my job and my pay stays bad. The two semi-autonomous drills probably stay at two, and I keep babysitting one with a tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do. Keep paying down the course loan, maybe finish it by next winter. Keep learning to code at night, because even small AI changes need someone who can talk to the software. And maybe ask for the next pay band, since I'm the one who trains people on the tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You train people on the tablet. Is that recognised in your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nope. It's, thanks Yara, you're a star. I'd use this picture to push for that to count, because it's real work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bored isn't a word I hear a lot. Why bored?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like learning stuff, and Kalder doesn't change much. If nothing big happens, I'd probably start looking at jobs at the remote operations centre in the city, just for something new.

S0.say: She'd say she isn't surprised because much of the AI talk is sales talk, but would still show colleagues how handy the tools are and might post a meme about it.
S0.think: She thinks this picture means she keeps her job but her pay stays low, still babysitting one semi-autonomous drill with a tablet.
S0.do: Keeps working, aims to pay off her course loan by next winter and keeps learning to code at night. Asks for the next pay band since she trains colleagues on the tablet.
S0.quote: Honestly, it means I keep my job and my pay stays bad.
S0.fieldNote: Yara is the rare person who finds the calm scenario a bit dull. She already does unpaid training work on the automated drills and wants it recognised in her pay. She'd consider moving for novelty, not out of fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's interesting. That's basically what's already starting at Kalder, just faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for anyone who wants to learn. I'd tell people at work not to wait, get on the tablet training now. I wouldn't blame anyone for being nervous, though, it's a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I'm already halfway there with the drills. The risk is that the company hires someone from the city with a computer degree instead of training people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to run three or four autonomous drills from one seat as soon as they offered it. I'd do the remote operator course in the first few months and ask the company to pay for a short automation certificate. I'd also apply at the remote centre in the city, just to see what they'd offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually a bit excited. It's the first time my job would get more interesting instead of more tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're calm, but you've got a week or two saved and few jobs nearby. Doesn't that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should, I know. But in this picture there's work, it's just different work, and I'm good at the different bit. If I were in the two-year one I'd say something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dean, who's been drilling for twenty-two years. He can tell what rock he's in by the sound, and the computer can't do that yet. I'd want them to keep him for the hard ground and not just push him out.

S1.say: She'd call it a chance for anyone willing to learn and tell colleagues to get on the tablet training now, while not blaming people for being nervous.
S1.think: She thinks she'd do well since she already supervises the semi-autonomous drills; the risk is the company hiring city graduates instead of training workers like her.
S1.do: Volunteers to run several autonomous drills from one seat, completes the remote operator course in the first months and asks the company to fund an automation certificate. Applies to the city remote centre to test her options.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, as her job would get more interesting rather than more tiring.
S1.quote: It's the first time my job would get more interesting instead of more tired.
S1.fieldNote: Yara sees steady change as an opening, and she acknowledged her thin savings when challenged but judged the risk manageable here. She is ready to bring in automation herself. She values an older colleague's skill that the machines can't yet match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whoa. Okay. Two years is a lot faster than I'd want, even me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to happen whether we like it or not, so let's be practical. Get people paid while they move, and get the training out fast. I'd probably be posting guides on what to learn, though I'd be guessing too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried for the first time. If AI can supervise the drills itself, then my tablet job's gone as well, and I've got a week of money and a loan. Being good at the new stuff doesn't help if the new stuff doesn't need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight for any job installing and setting up the new systems, because that's the last human bit for a while. I'd move to the city if that's where the job was, even sharing a room. I'd stop sending as much to my brother, which would kill me, and put every spare dollar on the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My heart's going a bit faster just saying it. But I'd still feel like I had moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother about the football money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd still pay for his boots but not the trip to the tournament. He's fifteen, he'd sulk for a day. Then he'd ask me to teach him to code, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the two years actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One shot at being one of the people who sets the robots up. That's it. In two years you don't change careers, you just jump onto the closest moving truck.

S2.say: She'd say it's going to happen anyway so people should be practical: pay workers while they move and roll out training fast. She'd post guides on what to learn while admitting she's guessing.
S2.think: She's worried for the first time, because AI could supervise the drills itself and she has a week of savings and a loan. Being good with new technology doesn't help if it doesn't need people.
S2.do: Goes straight for jobs installing and setting up the new systems and would move to the city for one. Cuts what she sends her brother and puts every spare dollar on her loan.
S2.feel: Anxious, with her heart beating faster, but still feeling she has moves.
S2.quote: In two years you don't change careers, you just jump onto the closest moving truck.
S2.fieldNote: Two years is the first scenario that worries Yara, because her edge disappears if machines supervise themselves. She still feels in control and plans to chase setup work. Cutting her brother's football money is the cost she minds most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. That's long enough to get really good at something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to train everyone who wants it, and I'd be pushing the company to run proper courses on site at Kalder. I'd probably offer to run a few myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I could get onto the setup and commissioning side, which is getting new systems working on site, and ride that wave until about 2031. After that, I don't know. Nobody does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do the automation certificate and push to join the team bringing in the new drills. I'd pay off the course loan by year two and then save properly, maybe two hundred a fortnight. I'd also keep learning to code, but properly this time, with a structured course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly because of the end bit. The middle part I'd actually enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay at Kalder or move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay while the new kit was going in, because that's where the learning is. Then I'd probably follow the work to whichever mine is next. I don't have a family or a mortgage, so moving is easy for me right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens on the day it arrives, in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'd want two things: some money saved and a name as someone who can make the machines work. If I've got both, I'd be all right for a while. If I've only got one, I'd be nervous.

S3.say: She'd say it's time to train everyone who wants it and push the company to run on-site courses, offering to teach some herself.
S3.think: She believes she could move into setup and commissioning work and ride that until 2031, but admits no one knows what comes after.
S3.do: Earns the automation certificate in year one and joins the team bringing in new drills. Pays off her course loan by year two, then saves about two hundred a fortnight and takes a structured coding course.
S3.feel: Uneasy about the end point, though she'd enjoy the years in between.
S3.quote: Uneasy, mostly because of the end bit. The middle part I'd actually enjoy.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Yara pictures herself as one of the people who installs the change, and she'd follow the work between mines. She judges her freedom from family ties as an advantage. Her worry is the unknown after 2031, not the transition itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Honestly, that's the one I'd pick if I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's not waste it. I'd want mining towns to get training centres now, not in 2035. Practical stuff, not speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have a good decade. I'd go from drilling to setting up autonomous gear to maybe managing a remote fleet. The last bit, when AI can do even that, I'd deal with when I'm closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, finish the loan and get the automation certificate. Then I'd look at a two-year technical diploma in automation or electrical, part-time, using AI as my tutor every night. I'd start saving properly too, aiming for three months of bills by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Which I know sounds strange, since it's the same ending. But ten years is a long time to get ready, and I'm good at getting ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said calm about the same ending. Is that really calm, or putting it off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair. Probably a bit of both. But I'm twenty-seven, and I've changed jobs twice already. I trust myself to change again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the ten years change compared with the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'm jumping onto any truck going. In 2036 I'm choosing the truck. That's a big difference for someone with no savings.

S4.say: She'd say there's time so it shouldn't be wasted, and would want practical training centres in mining towns now rather than speeches.
S4.think: She expects a good decade moving from drilling to autonomous setup and possibly managing a remote fleet, and would handle the final stage when it gets closer.
S4.do: Pays off her loan and gets the automation certificate in year one, then starts a part-time two-year technical diploma using AI as a nightly tutor. Aims to save three months of bills by year three.
S4.feel: Calm, though she admits it's partly putting off the same ending; she trusts herself to keep adapting.
S4.quote: In 2036 I'm choosing the truck. That's a big difference for someone with no savings.
S4.fieldNote: Yara stays calm even about the AGI end point given ten years, because she trusts her record of adapting. When pushed, she admitted it's partly avoidance. She ties the value of time directly to her lack of savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes away the one thing I'm good at, which is getting ready. What would help is paid training on site, fast, and some money to bridge people like me who don't have savings to fall back on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we'd want the robots to do. I'd love a robot to do the gravel-road drive at five in the morning. Start there.

headlineQuote: Being good at the new stuff doesn't help if the new stuff doesn't need people.
portrait: Yara Walsh is a 27-year-old blasthole drill operator at the Kalder iron ore mine, renting a room in Rookwood, paying off a course loan and sending money to her teenage brother, with a week or two of savings. She's practical and centrist, uses AI every day and already supervises a semi-autonomous drill from a tablet. A plateau bores her and steady change excites her, since her job would get more interesting. AGI in two years makes her anxious for the first time because her edge disappears, while five and ten years let her plan a path into automation work and stay mostly calm. She wants practical, paid training rather than speeches.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it takes away her ability to get ready, which is what she's good at.
whatWouldHelp: Fast, paid training on site and some money to bridge workers who don't have savings to fall back on.
